title: Packager
description: Move dust from your hand tool onto a conveyor. Check the $100 price, 100 kg storage and belt connection; this building is separate from the Auto-Packer upgrade.

sections.heading: What the Packager does
paragraphs: Unload collected dust at this transfer point and move it onward on a belt. It is not an autonomous cleaner or a processor. The Packager costs $100; the separate Building Tool costs $50.

sections.heading: Connect a useful route
paragraphs: Face the output toward a conveyor ending at a station intake or compatible processor. Load a small amount using the interaction prompt, then follow the capsules. A connected station pays; the Packager itself does not increase material value.

sections.heading: Storage and output
paragraphs: Storage holds 100 kg and outgoing capsules carry up to 1 kg. Output emission and belt capacity are separate limits, so an emission interval should not be mistaken for guaranteed route throughput.

sections.heading: Packager versus Auto-Packer
paragraphs: Auto-Packer is a separate $2,000 upgrade that drops a capsule when a hand-tool container fills. It does not build a conveyor connection and should not be counted as this $100 building.

title: Splitter
description: Split one capsule feed between two branches. Use the $5 Splitter to keep a raw-dust route available when another branch feeds a Pressure Chamber.

sections.heading: Routing role
paragraphs: The build price is $5. Splitters divide an incoming capsule route; they do not duplicate material. A downstream branch can only receive capsules supplied by the source.

sections.heading: Use with processing
paragraphs: A stone route needs both raw dust and sand. Preserve a dust branch instead of converting every capsule into sand. The practical division depends on actual supply and which machines are running.

sections.heading: Patch context
paragraphs: The developer fixed crewmate-built splitter and merger behavior in 1.0.3. Later notes allow players to add these devices to another crewmate’s belts. Check source and destination before diagnosing an old multiplayer bug.

title: Conveyor Belt
description: Connect tools, machines and the station intake with a belt. Check the price per metre, travel direction and capsule spacing before extending your route.

sections.heading: Length-based cost
paragraphs: Belts cost $0.50 per metre, not $0.50 for an arbitrary complete route. A 30 m straight segment therefore costs $15 before other equipment.

sections.heading: Transport limit
paragraphs: At 1.1 m/s with 0.75 m capsule spacing, the geometric limit is 88 capsules per minute. Busy merges, turns and a blocked destination can reduce the rate your route actually delivers.

sections.heading: Payment destination
paragraphs: Developer patch 1.0.3 confirms automatic payment for dust and stone arriving at the station deposit intake by belt. Finish the connection at the intake, rather than ending near the station.

title: Pressure Chamber
description: Convert dust into sand without changing its weight. Allow 10 kW of power and a clear outgoing belt, then check batch sizes before adding another chamber.

sections.heading: Full-power recipe
paragraphs: A full load is a maximum 5 kg batch taking 12 seconds at 10 kW. It preserves mass: dust becomes the same weight of sand. A full, continuously supplied chamber therefore makes 25 kg of sand per minute.

sections.heading: Value, not extra kilograms
paragraphs: The base sand price is $3/kg, compared with $1/kg dust. “3× value” does not mean 5 kg becomes 15 kg. At full batch size, output sales are $75/min and the dust’s base sale value is $25/min; the $50/min difference is processing value added, before infrastructure and downtime.

sections.heading: Power and partial batches
paragraphs: Smaller loads start after a short wait; insufficient power slows processing. Calculations here use full batches at full power. One 16 kW solar tracker covers the 10 kW nominal demand only under sufficient sunlight, with spare power and storage considered separately.

sections.heading: When adding stone production
paragraphs: A stone press consumes sand and fresh dust together. Keep an unprocessed dust supply. One chamber’s theoretical 25 kg/min sand output can supply 2.5 presses’ 10 kg/min sand demand, but this is a recipe ratio, not a complete ready-to-build line.

sections.heading: Partial loads, output and power cutoff
paragraphs: The chamber starts when 5 kg is loaded, or after waiting 3 seconds with a smaller load. It preserves the loaded mass when turning dust into sand.

The output emission interval is 0.35 seconds, separate from the production cycle. Processing stops below 8% of the required power. Belt spacing and a blocked destination can still limit outgoing flow.

title: Merger
description: Join two feeds with a $5 Merger that alternates between inputs. Both share one exit, so check the outgoing belt before adding more capsules upstream.

sections.heading: Combining routes
paragraphs: A Merger costs $5. It reduces the number of outgoing routes but does not increase the capacity of the single belt after it. Watch the shared exit when combining busy sources.

sections.heading: Input selection
paragraphs: The official 1.0.4 notes say mergers alternate between inputs. That behavior should not be described as a programmable priority rule. A blocked output can still queue both inputs.

sections.heading: A practical check
paragraphs: Test each source on its own, then enable both. If both work separately but queue together, inspect shared downstream capacity before replacing upstream machines.

title: Stone Press
description: Feed both raw dust and sand to make stone blocks. Plan for 18 kW of power, a six-second recipe cycle and space on the output belt before adding another press.

sections.heading: Two inputs, one stone block
paragraphs: The recipe takes 1 kg dust and 1 kg sand every 6 seconds, producing a single 2 kg block. At full power and continuous supply that is 10 blocks, or 20 kg, per minute. Nominal power demand is 18 kW.

sections.heading: Gross revenue and value added
paragraphs: At the $7/kg base stone price, one block sells for $14 and ideal output sales are $140/min. The consumed dust and sand could sell for $40/min at their base prices. The processing value added is therefore $100/min, not $140/min of extra value.

sections.heading: Reserve fresh dust
paragraphs: Feeding only sand leaves the other recipe input missing. Keep a raw-dust branch alongside the chamber’s sand branch. A solar tracker’s 16 kW peak is below the press’s 18 kW requirement; account for additional generation and night operation.

sections.heading: Pipeline limits
paragraphs: Two presses require 20 kg/min sand and 20 kg/min raw dust, plus the dust used by the sand chamber. Check both branches, output space and sustained power before relying on the theoretical rate.

sections.heading: Partial loads, output and power cutoff
paragraphs: The press needs both raw dust and sand. Its recipe produces one 2 kg block; a missing ingredient prevents a complete cycle.

The output emission interval is 0.35 seconds, separate from the production cycle. Processing stops below 8% of the required power. Belt spacing and a blocked destination can still limit outgoing flow.

title: Capsule Catcher
description: Receive J.O.O.N.A.S. deliveries in a 100 kg store. Keep the belt draining and check how nearby catchers share incoming capsules before expanding your robot fleet.

sections.heading: Receiving storage
paragraphs: The catcher costs $1,500 and stores 100 kg. Official patch 1.0.4 also confirms the 100 kg capacity. A catcher receives robot-launched capsules; it does not clean the surface itself.

sections.heading: With and without an output belt
paragraphs: Connect an output belt when you want the catcher to feed capsules into another route. Without that connection, check the station’s material and payment panels before relying on automatic sales. The timing of this no-belt path is unresolved in the linked documentation.

sections.heading: Distribution in 1.0.5
paragraphs: The developer groups catchers within 100 m. J.O.O.N.A.S. chooses the emptiest catcher in the nearest group, moving on when every catcher in that group is above 80% full.

title: Garage
description: Buy, recall and unload vehicles at the Garage. Check its $200 price and 6,000 kg silo, then connect a belt destination that can keep up with returning sweepers.

sections.heading: Vehicle hub
paragraphs: The garage costs $200, separate from vehicle purchase prices. Each player owns their purchased vehicles. Official 1.0.3 notes allow owned vehicles to be recalled, stored and upgraded through any garage.

sections.heading: Unloading versus outfeed
paragraphs: The collector-pad unloading rate is 600 kg/s into a 6,000 kg silo. This is not the rate at which a single conveyor can carry capsules away. A quickly emptied vehicle can still leave a growing silo queue.

sections.heading: Relocating a garage
paragraphs: Removing a garage no longer destroys the vehicles it stores according to patch 1.0.3. Check the output belts after relocating the base; 1.0.5 adds a status reason when the silo cannot send dust.

title: Solar Tracker (L)
description: Generate up to 16 kW in sunlight with a panel that follows the Sun. Check battery storage and connected demand before relying on it through the lunar night.

sections.heading: Output and wireless range
paragraphs: The $300 Solar Tracker follows the Sun, generates up to 16 kW and supplies machines within 34 m. Its 10 kWh battery stores energy for lower-generation periods.

sections.heading: Choose the connected machines
paragraphs: One Tracker can cover a 10 kW chamber in enough sunlight. It cannot cover an 18 kW press at nominal demand by itself. Add the load of every running machine within the powered area.

sections.heading: Store enough for night
paragraphs: At an ideal 10 kW load, a full 10 kWh battery represents one hour of energy. Actual uptime depends on charging, sunlight, available output and other machines. Peak generation is not an all-day average.

title: Solar Post (S)
description: Supply nearby equipment with a $75 fixed panel rated at 3 kW in full sun. Face it toward the Sun and keep consumers within 16 m; this panel has no battery.

sections.heading: Where the small panel fits
paragraphs: The $75 Solar Post supplies up to 3 kW within 16 m. It has no listed battery, so it cannot keep a powered processor running through darkness on its own.

sections.heading: Positioning and load
paragraphs: Face this fixed panel toward the Sun. A 10 kW chamber needs more than one small panel even at peak output. Compare total generation with the connected load.

sections.heading: Expanding a daytime supply
paragraphs: Use the small panel where its range and daytime output are enough. For continuous production, compare larger panels and their stored energy before building a dense group of small panels.

title: Solar Twin (M)
description: The $150 Solar Twin supplies up to 7.5 kW and stores 4 kWh. Face it toward the Sun and check the load within its 24 m range before leaving it to run at night.

sections.heading: Generation and storage
paragraphs: The $150 Solar Twin supplies up to 7.5 kW within 24 m and stores 4 kWh. Battery capacity is energy held for later, not extra peak generation.

sections.heading: Keep the panel facing sunlight
paragraphs: This model does not track the Sun. Placement affects how much daylight power it collects. Its peak output is below a chamber’s 10 kW nominal demand.

sections.heading: Plan the dark period
paragraphs: At an ideal 10 kW load, 4 kWh represents 24 minutes of energy. This is a capacity calculation, not a guarantee that the panel alone supplies the load. Include other machines and charging conditions.
